newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia says still committed to space station.
newsitem.headline: Russia says still committed to space station.

text.p: Russia said on Monday, following criticism from a senior U.S. lawmaker, that it remains committed to the planned Alpha international space station and has budgeted all the cash needed to fund its share of the project.
A government spokesman, Alexander Voznesensky, said funds for the project were included in the 1997 budget passed by the lower house of parliament on Friday.

"Russia will stay in the project, and Russia will fulfill all of its obligations accepted previously," he said. "The only thing is that there will be a small change in the timing given new obstacles."

James Sensenbrenner, the new chairman of the U.S. House of Representatives' Science Committee, said in an interview published in the New York Times on Monday that the project could unravel because Russia had been slow to meet its obligations.
But Voznesensky said that the interview did not take the passage of the budget into account.
He said the head of Russia's space agency, Yuri Koptev, would travel to the United States next Sunday and was ready to meet U.S. legislators to demonstrate Russia's commitment to the space station.
Russia has already built one module of the space station, but a second element -- the so-called service module where cosmonauts will live and work -- has fallen behind schedule.
Voznesensky said this module would be launched in November 1998 rather than in April as originally planned.
He expected Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and U.S. Vice President Al Gore to approve the delay in the launch when they meet in Washington on February 6 to 8.
Under plans worked out between Russia, the United States and other countries, the Alpha space station will be built in stages, with different parts arriving from November 1997.
A spokesman at the Khrunichev space centre in Moscow said workers were already building the service module.

"Last week we signed agreement with International Moscow Bank on a $35 million loan. He said part of this money would be used for work on the module, adding that the centre hoped to complete the module by July 1997.
Sensenbrenner had said Russia should be asked to cease being a full partner in the project if it was still withholding financing on the programme at the end of February.
A U.S. official familiar with the project said Russia's real problem now was putting parliament-approved funds to work.
"Allocating the money is only half the battle," the official said, adding that there was "a long step between the allocation and getting the money to the contracters".

Once a priority of the Soviet state, Russia's space industry has fallen upon hard times, along with many other sectors of the economy. Koptev said last week it would cost 1.5 trillion rubles ($270 million) to complete the space station module.
